title: Double Modular Exponentiation
summary: Given a 0-indexed 2D array variables with each row as [ai, bi, ci, mi], and an integer target, identify indices i where 0 <= i < variables.length and ((ai^bi % 10)^ci) % mi equals target.
statement: Given a 0-indexed 2D array variables with each row as [ai, bi, ci, mi], and an integer target, identify indices i where 0 <= i < variables.length and ((ai^bi % 10)^ci) % mi equals target. Return an array of these indices in any order.
constraints: Each row is [a,b,c,m] with positive integers, and target is nonnegative.
Index i is good when ((a^b mod 10)^c) mod m equals target.
Return all good zero-based indices in any order.
reference_solution:
def double_modular_good_indices(variables,target):
    return [index for index,(a,b,c,modulus) in enumerate(variables) if pow(pow(a,b,10),c,modulus)==target]
hints: Modular exponentiation must be applied in two separate stages, with modulus ten first.
Use three-argument pow for both exponentiations and retain matching row indices.
For each [a,b,c,m], compute inner=pow(a,b,10), then pow(inner,c,m), and compare with target.
Each computation matches the formula exactly while modular exponentiation avoids constructing enormous powers.
editorial: Each computation matches the formula exactly while modular exponentiation avoids constructing enormous powers.

tests.explanation: Rows zero and two evaluate to two; row one evaluates to zero.
The inner remainder is nine and nine to the thousandth modulo one thousand is one, so no index qualifies.
